processing: A green tea finished either flat and straight or in fine tight strips, across a range that includes a pan-fired line. Exact steps are not published.
harvest_season: No picking calendar is published for this tea; in the wider Longnan area picking starts in late March to early April, and the first spring tea is usually the most valued.
appearance_dry: Flat and straight or fine and tight, an emerald green.
appearance_liquor: Clear and bright; as with other Longnan greens, usually a light green-yellow.
appearance_wet: As with other Longnan greens, young whole leaf and bud in a soft green.
taste_profile: Mellow and refreshing with a clean mouthfeel and a chestnut note.

brewing.notes: General guidance for a Chinese green rather than a local rule: slightly cooler water keeps the chestnut note clean.

vintage_note: As with other Chinese greens, it is sold as a current-year harvest and is best within about a year. The range comes in many named lines and grades, such as Cuifeng, Cuizhu and Yinhao, so check which one you are buying as well as the harvest date.
description:
Longshen Tea is a green tea from the Longshen gully in the Yangba tea area of Kangxian, far southeast Gansu, a pocket promoted as the Jiangnan of Gansu. The protected zone is unusually small: just four villages, Yezi Ba, Chayuan, Wukeshi and Laozhuang.

In practice it is closely tied to one producer, Gansu Longshen Tea Co., which has sold it under the Kangyang brand among others. Its six or so product lines run from Cuifeng and Yinhao to an everyday pan-fired tea, so the name covers quite different leaves.

The leaf is emerald and the taste mellow and refreshing with a note of chestnut. As with other Longnan greens, keep the water just below boiling and do not oversteep.

The lines most often named are Longshen Cuifeng and Cuizhu, which have collected tea competition awards. Treat them as the place to start, and check the harvest date as you would with any green.
history:
The Kangyang brand was certified organic in 2003, and the Cuifeng and Cuizhu lines won awards at international famous tea contests.

The tea also holds national geographical indication protection, with its area defined following a 2006 proposal by the Kangxian government. Its earlier history is little documented.
